Unit 1: From oscillation estimates to pointwise convergence through all lengths

This unit studies §3 of C. Proposition 3.5 is taken as the specified analytic input, and the subsequent convergence argument is developed in detail. The source passages are Definition 3.1 (p.5), Proposition 3.5 (pp.8–9), Lemmas 3.6–3.9 (pp.9–12), and the proof of the main theorem at the end of §3 (pp.12–13).

1. The conclusion, reductions, and specified input

Source: C Theorem 1.1, p.1.

Let (X,F,μ)(X,\mathcal F,\mu)(X,F,μ) be a probability space, and let TTT be invertible, bimeasurable, probability-preserving, and mixing. Fix three pairwise distinct nonzero integers λ1,λ2,λ3\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3λ1​,λ2​,λ3​ and functions f1,f2,f3∈L∞(μ)f_1,f_2,f_3\in L^\infty(\mu)f1​,f2​,f3​∈L∞(μ). The paper claims that

almost everywhere, as NNN runs through all positive integers.

This unit proves that the conclusion follows from the oscillation estimate below. In the paper, that estimate is deduced from C Theorem 2.2 and Lemmas 3.2–3.4. Those results, together with the relevant proofs in H and D, are left for later discussion.

1.4 Proposition 3.5: The assumed oscillation estimate

Source: the statement at the end of C p.8 and its proof on p.9; the conclusion is equation (3.11).

Fix the slopes above and one averaging weight φ\varphiφ. The paper claims that there is a constant Cφ,b<∞C_{\varphi,b}\lt\inftyCφ,b​<∞ such that, for every integer w≥1w\ge1w≥1 and every deterministic sequence of integer endpoints

0≤k1<k2<⋯<kw+1 0\le k_1\lt k_2\lt\cdots\lt k_{w+1} 0≤k1​<k2​<⋯<kw+1​

we have

∑i=1w∫Xmax⁡ki≤ℓ≤ki+1∣Vℓφ(x)−Vkiφ(x)∣ dμ(x)≤Cφ,bw.(O) \sum_{i=1}^{w} \int_X \max_{k_i\le\ell\le k_{i+1}} |V_\ell^\varphi(x)-V_{k_i}^\varphi(x)| \,\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \le C_{\varphi,b}\sqrt w. \tag{O} i=1∑w​∫X​ki​≤ℓ≤ki+1​max​∣Vℓφ​(x)−Vki​φ​(x)∣dμ(x)≤Cφ,b​w​.(O)

Here SSS need only be invertible, bimeasurable, and probability-preserving; neither ergodicity nor mixing is required. The functions are normalized by ∣fj∣≤1|f_j|\le1∣fj​∣≤1. The constant may depend on the fixed slopes and weight, but not on the system, functions, endpoints, or number of blocks www.

“Deterministic endpoints” means that the same kik_iki​ are used for every xxx. The maximizing position may depend on xxx, but each maximum is taken over finitely many scales, so its integrand is measurable. These two facts are compatible.

Estimate (O) is not treated here as an established classical theorem. It is the crucial input claimed by the manuscript and still to be verified. Its stated derivation runs through the local depth-varying estimate C Theorem 2.2 (pp.3–4), the cancellation kernel in C Lemma 3.2 (p.6), the real-line estimate C Lemma 3.3 (p.7), the integer-sequence estimate C Lemma 3.4 (pp.7–8), and finally finite-orbit transference.

2. Why oscillation rules out nonconvergence on a set of positive measure

Source: C Lemma 3.6, pp.9–10. We first formulate the assertion for an abstract sequence of functions.

2.1 The full statement

Let (Zk)k≥0(Z_k)_{k\ge0}(Zk​)k≥0​ be a uniformly bounded sequence of measurable complex-valued functions on a probability space. Suppose there is a constant CCC such that, for every w≥1w\ge1w≥1 and every deterministic sequence of endpoints 0≤k1<⋯<kw+10\le k_1\lt\cdots\lt k_{w+1}0≤k1​<⋯<kw+1​,

∑i=1w∫Xmax⁡ki≤ℓ≤ki+1∣Zℓ−Zki∣ dμ≤Cw. \sum_{i=1}^{w}\int_X \max_{k_i\le\ell\le k_{i+1}} |Z_\ell-Z_{k_i}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu \le C\sqrt w. i=1∑w​∫X​ki​≤ℓ≤ki+1​max​∣Zℓ​−Zki​​∣dμ≤Cw​.

Then Zk(x)Z_k(x)Zk​(x) converges on a measurable set of full measure. The conclusion specifies neither the limit nor a rate of convergence.

{ω>0}=⋃m=1∞{ω>2/m}, \{\omega>0\}=\bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}\{\omega>2/m\}, {ω>0}=m=1⋃∞​{ω>2/m},

2.4 Linear lower growth versus a square-root upper bound

Source: p.10, the last three sentences of the proof of Lemma 3.6.

Start with k1=0k_1=0k1​=0. At each step, use the previous endpoint as the new KKK and choose the next endpoint by (B). This produces deterministic, strictly increasing endpoints, with the same lower bound δd/2\delta d/2δd/2 on every block. Consequently, for every www,

wδd2≤∑i=1w∫Xmax⁡ki≤ℓ≤ki+1∣Zℓ−Zki∣ dμ≤Cw. \frac{w\delta d}{2} \le\sum_{i=1}^{w}\int_X \max_{k_i\le\ell\le k_{i+1}}|Z_\ell-Z_{k_i}| \,\mathrm{d}\mu \le C\sqrt w. 2wδd​≤i=1∑w​∫X​ki​≤ℓ≤ki+1​max​∣Zℓ​−Zki​​∣dμ≤Cw​.

Thus w≤2C/(δd)\sqrt w\le2C/(\delta d)w​≤2C/(δd). The right side is fixed, whereas www can be arbitrarily large, a contradiction. Hence ω=0\omega=0ω=0 almost everywhere, which proves the assertion.

Apply this to Zk=VkφZ_k=V_k^\varphiZk​=Vkφ​, using (O) and the uniform bound from §1.3. The smooth averages for each fixed weight converge almost everywhere. Mixing has not been used.

2.5 Why sublinear growth matters

A bound of only CwCwCw would not suffice. For example, Zk(x)=(−1)kZ_k(x)=(-1)^kZk​(x)=(−1)k is independent of xxx. Its maximal oscillation on each integer block with distinct endpoints is 222, so the total is 2w2w2w, but the sequence does not converge. What matters is sublinear growth uniformly over all choices of endpoints.

Even if each point continues to make excursions, no single excursion time need work for every point. Taking a finite maximum before integrating avoids this error in the order of quantifiers.

3. Multiple L2L^2L2 convergence from ordinary mixing

Source: C Lemmas 3.7–3.8, pp.10–11. We state the norm-convergence theorem for any finite number of factors. In the present triple-average application, the transformation is SSS.

Let (X,F,μ)(X,\mathcal F,\mu)(X,F,μ) be a probability space, and let TTT be invertible, bimeasurable, probability-preserving, and mixing. Fix an integer d≥1d\ge1d≥1, pairwise distinct nonzero integers a1,…,ada_1,\ldots,a_da1​,…,ad​, and functions f1,…,fd∈L∞(μ)f_1,\ldots,f_d\in L^\infty(\mu)f1​,…,fd​∈L∞(μ). Then

1N∑n=1N∏j=1dfj∘Tajn⟶∏j=1d∫Xfj dμin L2(μ). \frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\prod_{j=1}^d f_j\circ T^{a_jn} \longrightarrow\prod_{j=1}^d\int_Xf_j\,\mathrm{d}\mu \quad\text{in }L^2(\mu). N1​n=1∑N​j=1∏d​fj​∘Taj​n⟶j=1∏d​∫X​fj​dμin L2(μ).

This is a norm-convergence statement. It does not directly yield almost-everywhere convergence through all lengths, and it is distinct from higher-order mixing without time averaging.

3.1 From mixing of sets to correlations of functions

Source: C p.10, the beginning of §3.3 and equation (3.13).

Mixing of sets asserts that, for fixed E,F∈FE,F\in\mathcal FE,F∈F, we have μ(E∩T−mF)→μ(E)μ(F)\mu(E\cap T^{-m}F)\to\mu(E)\mu(F)μ(E∩T−mF)→μ(E)μ(F) as ∣m∣→∞|m|\to\infty∣m∣→∞. We need to deduce that, for fixed bounded measurable functions g,hg,hg,h,

∫Xg(h∘Tm) dμ⟶(∫Xg dμ)(∫Xh dμ). \int_Xg(h\circ T^m)\,\mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow \left(\int_Xg\,\mathrm{d}\mu\right) \left(\int_Xh\,\mathrm{d}\mu\right). ∫X​g(h∘Tm)dμ⟶(∫X​gdμ)(∫X​hdμ).

If g,hg,hg,h are simple functions, express them as finite linear combinations of indicator functions. The integral on the left expands into finitely many set correlations, and the conclusion follows term by term from the definition.

In general, for each ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, choose simple functions gε,hεg_\varepsilon,h_\varepsilongε​,hε​ with ∥g−gε∥∞≤ε\|g-g_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le\varepsilon∥g−gε​∥∞​≤ε and ∥h−hε∥∞≤ε\|h-h_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le\varepsilon∥h−hε​∥∞​≤ε. Such uniform approximations follow by dividing the bounded complex ranges into finitely many small cells. For every mmm,

∣∫gh∘Tm−∫gεhε∘Tm∣≤ε∥h∥∞+(∥g∥∞+ε)ε. \left|\int gh\circ T^m-\int g_\varepsilon h_\varepsilon\circ T^m\right| \le\varepsilon\|h\|_\infty+(\|g\|_\infty+\varepsilon)\varepsilon. ​∫gh∘Tm−∫gε​hε​∘Tm​≤ε∥h∥∞​+(∥g∥∞​+ε)ε.

The difference between the corresponding products of integrals has the same upper bound. Fix ε\varepsilonε, apply the simple-function conclusion as ∣m∣→∞|m|\to\infty∣m∣→∞, and then let ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0ε↓0. This proves the required function formulation. Complex coefficients cause no change in the argument.

3.4 Assumptions and order of limits

  • Distinct slopes ensure that the difference slopes in the induction are nonzero.
  • Each slope is nonzero, so ∣ajh∣→∞|a_jh|\to\infty∣aj​h∣→∞ and mixing applies.
  • Invertibility permits negative times and the measure-preserving change of variables.
  • Boundedness places every product in L2L^2L2 and controls the finitely many terms deleted for fixed hhh.
  • First fix hhh, then let N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞. In (H), first fix HHH and only at the end let H→∞H\to\inftyH→∞. No rate of mixing is needed.

The slope conditions cannot be dropped. For instance, with two equal slopes and f2=f1‾f_2=\overline{f_1}f2​=f1​​, the average is an ordinary ergodic average of ∣f1∣2|f_1|^2∣f1​∣2, whose limit is generally not ∣∫f1∣2|\int f_1|^2∣∫f1​∣2. If a zero slope is allowed and the other function is identically one, the zero-slope observable retains its dependence on the starting point.

5.2 Stability of the derivative class under fixed operations

Source: C p.5, the paragraph on closure properties following Definition 3.1.

A fixed translation leaves the derivative supremum norms unchanged. For a fixed scale a>0a>0a>0 and a fixed center zzz,

drdtr[a−1ρ(t/a−z)]=a−r−1ρ(r)(t/a−z). \frac{\mathrm{d}^r}{\mathrm{d}t^r} \left[a^{-1}\rho(t/a-z)\right] =a^{-r-1}\rho^{(r)}(t/a-z). dtrdr​[a−1ρ(t/a−z)]=a−r−1ρ(r)(t/a−z).

A fixed dilation therefore introduces a factor growing at most exponentially in rrr, which can be absorbed by increasing GGG. Differentiation of a fixed order replaces rrr by r+mr+mr+m. The word “fixed” is important: no single GGG has been obtained uniformly over all translation parameters, scales, or linear combinations.

5.7 Why the expanding support matters

The support of ρi,A\rho_{i,A}ρi,A​ lies in A[zi−1,zi+1]A[z_i-1,z_i+1]A[zi​−1,zi​+1]. Higher accuracy may require larger AAA, and hence larger supports for the correction terms. Their L1L^1L1 mass is O(A−1)O(A^{-1})O(A−1), whereas their jjj-th moments may be amplified by AjA^jAj. A small L1L^1L1 change can therefore correct the low-order moments exactly.

If instead every approximant were required to be supported in the same interval [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R], then

∣∫t2(φ−hc) dt∣≤R2∥φ−hc∥1 \left|\int t^2(\varphi-h_c)\,\mathrm{d}t\right| \le R^2\|\varphi-h_c\|_1 ​∫t2(φ−hc​)dt​≤R2∥φ−hc​∥1​

For R≥cR\ge cR≥c, this would force the second moments to converge as the L1L^1L1 error tends to zero. But ∫t2φ=0\int t^2\varphi=0∫t2φ=0, whereas ∫t2hc=c2/3>0\int t^2h_c=c^2/3>0∫t2hc​=c2/3>0, a contradiction. A common fixed support cannot be added to the approximation statement. The paper does not impose one.

7. What has been established in this unit

Conditional on Proposition 3.5, the argument is complete in the following order:

  1. The uniform bound and oscillation estimate imply almost-everywhere convergence of the smooth averages for each fixed averaging weight.
  2. Ordinary mixing and the finite Hilbert-space inequality imply that the ordinary averages with distinct nonzero integer slopes converge in L2L^2L2 to the product of the integrals.
  3. Abel summation for positive and negative times shows that the same smooth averages converge in L2L^2L2 to that product. Fatou's lemma identifies the pointwise limit.
  4. Weights with the prescribed derivative bounds and vanishing moments approximate the interval weight in L1L^1L1.
  5. One countable intersection of full-measure sets covers the dyadic scales with all rational ratios. A finite grid and the length-comparison estimate recover all integers.

Proposition 3.5 itself and the local analytic estimates on which it depends have not been proved in this unit. The next task is to check the uniformity of C Theorem 2.2 in depth, number of blocks, and changes of input, and to inspect the exact results invoked from H and D.

The higher-order mixing assertion in R plays no part in this L2L^2L2 proof. It is a separate dependency of B and A. Combining the two arguments into the claim that “mixing makes everything independent” would misstate the proof.

8. Questions for further discussion

  • If the oscillation bound held only for one predetermined sequence of endpoints, would the recursive block selection in §2 still be possible?
  • If CCC were allowed to depend on www, where would the argument fail?
  • Why does the norm-convergence proof fix the correlation gap hhh before sending the averaging length NNN to infinity?
  • Which partial sums handle the negative-time support of the smooth weight in Abel summation?
  • Why does L1L^1L1 approximation of a positive interval weight not force the corrected signed weight to have a similar second moment?
  • Why is there no need in §6 to intersect the full-measure sets for all real ccc?
  • If convergence were known only for N=2kN=2^kN=2k, why would the length-comparison estimate (L) not immediately send the remaining error to zero?
